description: From Bournemouth's Vitality Stadium to Bodø/Glimt's 8,270-seat Aspmyra. The smallest stadiums hosting top-level professional football.
keywords: smallest stadiums in football, smallest professional football stadiums, Vitality Stadium capacity, Aspmyra Bodø Glimt, smallest top flight stadium, small football grounds
h1: The Smallest Stadiums in Professional Football
lead: Not every top-flight club plays in a colossus. Some of the smallest stadiums in professional football hold fewer than the crowd at a big high-school game in the United States.
thumbCaption: The smallest stadiums in professional football
share: An 8,270-seat Champions League stadium and an 11,307-seat Premier League ground — the smallest stadiums in professional football.
content:
When we picture professional football we picture cauldrons of 60,000 and 90,000. But plenty of clubs play at a very different scale. Across the top divisions of Europe, there are grounds so small that every seat in the house is close to the pitch — and the atmosphere is often better for it.

The Smallest Premier League Stadium

The smallest stadium in the English Premier League is the Vitality Stadium in Bournemouth, home of AFC Bournemouth. It holds just 11,307 people, making it comfortably the most compact ground in the division. When Bournemouth won promotion to the Premier League in 2015, they took a stadium that had spent most of its life as a lower-league ground into the biggest league in the world — and stayed there, largely because the tiny, packed terraces create a ferocious home atmosphere.

The Smallest in Each Major League

Across the five big European leagues, the smallest stadiums are a mix of newly promoted clubs and long-established communities:

LeagueStadiumClubCapacity
Premier LeagueVitality StadiumAFC Bournemouth11,307
La LigaEstadi Johan CruyffBarcelona B / women's6,000
BundesligaVoith-ArenaHeidenheim15,000
Serie ACetilar ArenaPisa12,508
Ligue 1Stade Francis-Le BléBrest15,931

The Estadi Johan Cruyff is a special case: it is the 6,000-seat home of Barcelona's reserve and women's teams, which means the smallest ground attached to a truly elite club sits a stone's throw from the 99,354-seat Camp Nou.

The Smallest Champions League Stadium

The most extreme example in recent European football is Aspmyra, the home of Norway's Bodø/Glimt, with a capacity of around 8,270. That is the smallest stadium to host a Champions League campaign in modern times. Bodø/Glimt famously beat Roma 6-1 there in the 2021 Europa Conference League and reached the Champions League group stage in 2024, forcing Europe's giants to play in a compact Arctic arena where the wind and the crowd do the defending.

Gibraltar's Miniature National Stadium

At the very bottom of the professional scale sits Victoria Stadium in Gibraltar, home to the country's national team and its domestic league. Depending on how it is configured it holds somewhere between roughly 2,000 and 5,000 people. Gibraltar's clubs — including Lincoln Red Imps — play their entire league and European seasons there, and national team matches against giants like England and Spain take place in front of a crowd smaller than many youth finals.

Why Small Grounds Produce Big Noise

Small stadiums are often dismissed as a handicap, but there is a counter-argument. With every spectator close to the action, the noise is concentrated, and the intimidation factor can be huge. It is no coincidence that the loudest crowds recorded in football — which we rank in our loudest crowds guide — come from relatively compact, steeply banked stadiums rather than the enormous ones.

The trade-off: A small stadium means less matchday revenue, but it also means no empty seats, an intimate atmosphere and a genuine home advantage. For clubs like Bodø/Glimt, it has become part of the identity — and part of the plan.

title: The Loudest Football Crowds Ever Recorded | WinFulltime
description: Beşiktaş hit 132 dB and Galatasaray reached 131.76 dB. The Guinness crowd roar record is 142.2 dB — set in an NFL game. Football's loudest crowds, ranked.
keywords: loudest football crowds, loudest crowd decibels, loudest stadium in the world, Galatasaray 131.76 dB, Besiktas 132 dB, Guinness loudest crowd record, football atmosphere noise
h1: The Loudest Football Crowds Ever Recorded
lead: Decibel meters have been taken into the stands, and the results are astonishing. These are the loudest football crowds ever recorded — and the stadiums engineered to deafen.
thumbCaption: The loudest football crowds ever recorded
share: 132 decibels in Istanbul, 129 in Glasgow. The loudest football crowds ever recorded, ranked by the meters.
content:
Every fan believes their stadium is the loudest. In a few cases, the claim has actually been measured. Decibel meters placed in the stands have produced a definitive, if noisy, ranking of football's loudest crowds — and the results cluster in one country above all.

The World Record Is Not Football

Before ranking football, an honest disclaimer: the all-time Guinness World Record for the loudest crowd roar belongs to American football, not soccer. At Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City on 29 September 2014, Kansas City Chiefs fans produced 142.2 decibels during a game against the New England Patriots. The record still stands, and no football ground has come close to matching it — the sport's stadiums are smaller, and its roofs are less enclosed.

Football's Own Loudest Crowds

Within football, the records cluster in Istanbul. Turkish grounds are built like bowls, with steep stands that trap sound, and derbies between the Istanbul giants push crowds to extremes.

Club / stadiumDecibelsWhen
Beşiktaş, Vodafone Park132 dB2007
Galatasaray, Türk Telekom Arena131.76 dB2011
Fenerbahçe, Şükrü Saracoğlu131 dB2010s
Celtic, Celtic Park129 dB2024
Everton, new stadium126 dB2025

Galatasaray's 131.76 dB reading, recorded during a derby against Fenerbahçe in 2011, was for a time the official Guinness crowd-roar record for a football match — until newer readings and the NFL record reshuffled the charts. For comparison, 130 decibels is roughly the volume of a jet engine taking off at close range.

Why Turkish Stadiums Are So Loud

There is a reason Istanbul dominates the list. The Türk Telekom Arena (now RAMS Park) was deliberately built as a sound trap, with steep, enclosed stands designed to bounce noise back onto the pitch. Add the intense rivalry of the Istanbul derby — where fans sing, drum and whistle for the full 90 minutes — and the physics of the ground do the rest. Football's loudest crowd is not a coincidence; it is architecture.

Celtic Park and the 'Loudest in Britain'

Scotland's Celtic Park regularly claims the title of the loudest stadium in Britain, with a reading of 129 dB recorded during a Champions League night in 2024. The combination of the Celtic support's famous singing culture and the stadium's steep, enclosed design produces a wall of sound that visiting teams routinely describe as intimidating.

For context: A normal conversation is around 60 dB, a rock concert around 110 dB, and 120 dB sits at the edge of physical pain. Football's loudest crowds are hitting the same numbers as the loudest concerts on Earth — for ninety minutes at a time.

Can Football Ever Beat the NFL Record?

To match Arrowhead's 142.2 dB, a football crowd would need a stadium with a fully enclosed roof and an even bigger crowd. The two candidates most often discussed are Istanbul's giant new venues and a packed Rungrado stadium — but as of now, the football record remains a Turkish one, and the all-sport record remains in Kansas City.

title: The Most Famous Football Derbies in the World | WinFulltime
description: El Clásico, Old Firm, Superclásico and Merseyside. The most famous football derbies in the world and what makes each one special.
keywords: most famous football derbies, El Clasico, Old Firm, Superclasico Boca River, Merseyside derby, Manchester derby, Milan derby, football rivalries
h1: The Most Famous Football Derbies in the World
lead: Some matches are just fixtures. Others are events that stop a city, divide a country and define a season. These are the most famous football derbies on Earth.
thumbCaption: The most famous football derbies in the world
share: From El Clásico to the Old Firm — the most famous football derbies in the world, ranked.
content:
In football, a derby is more than a game between local rivals. It is identity, history and grievance condensed into ninety minutes. Across the world, a handful of derbies have outgrown their cities entirely, drawing global audiences and producing some of the most intense atmospheres the sport can create.

El Clásico: Real Madrid vs Barcelona

The most watched club fixture in the world pits Real Madrid against Barcelona. It is far more than a football match: for decades it has carried political and cultural weight, with Barcelona seen as the symbol of Catalonia against the capital's establishment club. With over 250 official meetings, both clubs have produced the two greatest rivalries in modern football history — and the two greatest players of the era, Messi and Ronaldo, defined the fixture for a decade.

The Old Firm: Celtic vs Rangers

Glasgow's Old Firm is the most intense derby in the British Isles, and one of the most watched in the world. The clubs' rivalry began with the very first meeting on 28 May 1888, and it has always carried more than sport — religion, politics and history all feed into it. The term 'Old Firm' dates from 1904, coined for the money-spinning matches between the two Glasgow giants. Between them they have won virtually every Scottish title since the 1890s, and their meetings still stop the country.

The Superclásico: Boca Juniors vs River Plate

In Argentina, the Superclásico between Buenos Aires rivals Boca Juniors and River Plate is routinely described as the most ferocious derby in world football. The two clubs share the same city but represent opposing sides of the divide: Boca historically the club of the working-class south, River the more affluent north. Their matches are famous for flares, tifo, noise and the most intense man-marking in the sport. The Superclásico has been named by many publications the greatest derby on Earth.

The Milan Derby: Inter vs AC Milan

Italy's Derby della Madonnina — named for the statue of the Virgin Mary atop Milan Cathedral — is one of Europe's most storied fixtures. Inter and AC Milan share the San Siro, which means the derby is decided in the same stadium twice a year. The two clubs have combined for dozens of Serie A titles and European Cups, and the derby has featured the likes of Maldini, Baresi, Ronaldo (the Brazilian) and Ibrahimović.

The English Derbies

England has a rich collection of its own. The Merseyside derby between Liverpool and Everton is the longest continuously played top-flight derby in the country, first played in 1894 and famous for its intensity despite the clubs' shared city. The North London derby between Arsenal and Tottenham, and the Manchester derby between United and City — transformed since City's takeover into a genuine title rivalry — complete the modern English landscape. The Steel City derby between Sheffield United and Sheffield Wednesday is the oldest of them all, first played in the 1890s.

Europe's Other Great Derbies

Across Europe, three more derbies deserve a place in the top tier:

  • Der Klassiker — Bayern Munich vs Borussia Dortmund, the modern Bundesliga's defining rivalry.
  • Derby d'Italia — Juventus vs Inter, the two most successful Italian clubs.
  • De Klassieker — Ajax vs Feyenoord, the Netherlands' biggest fixture.
DerbyTeamsWhy it matters
El ClásicoReal Madrid vs BarcelonaPolitical weight + global superstars
Old FirmCeltic vs RangersScottish dominance + history
SuperclásicoBoca vs RiverFiercest atmosphere on Earth
Derby della MadonninaInter vs AC MilanShared stadium, endless titles
Merseyside derbyLiverpool vs EvertonOldest continuous top-flight derby
Derbies are different: Form goes out of the window. In derbies, form, league position and even quality matter far less than desire — which is why football betting markets price derbies so cautiously.

keywords: oldest football rivalry, Sheffield FC Hallam 1860, Old Firm 1888, oldest derby in the world, Steel City derby, oldest football fixtures
h1: The Oldest Football Rivalries Still Played Today
lead: Some rivalries predate most countries. These are the oldest football rivalries in the world — fixtures that were being played before the modern game even had rules.
thumbCaption: The oldest football rivalries still played today
share: A derby that began in 1860 and the Old Firm in 1888 — the oldest rivalries football still plays today.
content:
Rivalries are football's oldest tradition. Long before leagues, cups or television, two teams were meeting over and over again because they lived on the same street and refused to lose to each other. Some of those fixtures are still played today, making them the oldest continuously existing rivalries in the sport.

The Rules Derby: Sheffield FC vs Hallam FC

The oldest football rivalry in the world is between the two oldest clubs in the world. Sheffield FC, founded in 1857, and Hallam FC, founded in 1860, first met on 26 December 1860 in the world's very first inter-club football match. Sheffield won 2-0 at Sandygate — which is still the world's oldest football ground.

For more than 160 years the pair have kept meeting, and the fixture — now nicknamed the Rules Derby — still takes place in Sheffield's lower leagues today. In January 2025 they even played a competitive match again for the first time in years, a meeting of the two founding fathers of world football.

The Old Firm: Celtic vs Rangers

Scotland's Old Firm began on 28 May 1888, when Celtic — in their very first match as a club — beat Rangers 5-2 in a friendly. From that first meeting, the rivalry grew into the defining fixture of Scottish football. The 'Old Firm' label was coined around 1904, and the two clubs have contested the Scottish title between them for over a century, making it one of the oldest and most played rivalries in the history of the sport.

The Steel City Derby

England's oldest professional league rivalry is the Steel City Derby between Sheffield United and Sheffield Wednesday. The two clubs first met in the 1890s, and their fixture is routinely listed as the oldest derby in the English Football League — older than the Merseyside or Manchester derbies. Sheffield's unique place in football history — home to both the oldest clubs and the first football association — makes the city the cradle of the sport's rivalries as well.

How Old Are the Other Great Derbies?

The biggest international derbies are centuries-fresh compared with the Sheffield rivals, but still older than many national leagues:

RivalryFirst meetingAge today
Sheffield FC vs Hallam1860165+ years
Celtic vs Rangers1888135+ years
Sheffield United vs Wednesday1890s130+ years
Liverpool vs Everton1894130+ years
Real Madrid vs Barcelona1902120+ years
Boca Juniors vs River Plate1913110+ years

What Keeps a Rivalry Alive for a Century?

Football historians point to three ingredients that turn a fixture into a rivalry that outlasts generations:

  • Geography — clubs that share a city or region meet constantly, so the results keep stacking up.
  • Identity — rivals usually stand for something different: class, district, religion or politics.
  • Stakes — when the two clubs compete for the same trophies, every meeting matters.
The bottom line: The oldest rivalry still played is the Rules Derby, Sheffield FC against Hallam FC, first contested in 1860. Everything else in football — every derby, every grudge match — descends from that first kick at Sandygate.

title: The Most Unusual Football Club Nicknames | WinFulltime
description: The Tangerines, the Addicks, the Pies and the Baggies. The most unusual football club nicknames and the strange stories behind them.
keywords: football club nicknames, unusual football nicknames, Charlton Addicks, West Brom Baggies, Leicester Foxes, Sheffield Wednesday Owls, strange club nicknames
h1: The Most Unusual Football Club Nicknames
lead: Every club has a nickname, but some are stranger than others. Behind the Tangerines and the Owls lie stories about fishmongers, foundry workers and a monkey mascot.
thumbCaption: The most unusual football club nicknames
share: Why are West Brom the Baggies and Charlton the Addicks? The strangest football club nicknames, explained.
content:
A club's nickname is its second identity — the word fans sing in the stands and print on scarves. Most are predictable (the Reds, the Blues, the Lions). But a significant number of the world's most established clubs answer to something genuinely baffling, and every strange nickname has a story behind it.

The Addicks of Charlton

Why is London club Charlton Athletic known as the Addicks? The story goes back to the early 1900s and a local fishmonger named Arthur Bryan, whose cry of 'haddock' — heard every Saturday on the terraces and rendered in the local accent — became the club's nickname. The fish eventually turned up on the club crest, making the Addicks one of football's great accidental nicknames.

The Baggies of West Brom

West Bromwich Albion are the Baggies, and the name has nothing to do with bags. In the early 20th century the club's supporters worked in the local foundries, and their baggy work trousers — tied tight at the ankle — became their trademark look on the terraces. 'The Baggies' stuck, and a century later the club's fans still answer to it.

The Foxes of Leicester

Leicester City are the Foxes because Leicestershire is fox-hunting country. The fox appeared on the club crest in 1948 and has been there ever since. But the club had two stranger earlier nicknames: the Fossils (from their original name, Leicester Fosse) and the Filberts — after Filbert Street, their old home and a type of hazelnut.

The Owls of Sheffield Wednesday

Sheffield Wednesday were known as the Blades — like their rivals Sheffield United — until 1912, when the club's new mascot, a live owl, arrived at Hillsborough. The Owl replaced the previous mascot, which had been a monkey, and the nickname switched with it. That is how one of England's biggest clubs came to be named after a bird.

The Tangerines of Blackpool

Blackpool are the Tangerines because of their bright orange kit — a colour the club adopted after a director was impressed by the Netherlands national team's orange shirts. The alternative nickname, the Seasiders, is far more predictable for a club from a seaside town.

More Strange Nicknames, Explained

The list of genuinely unusual club nicknames goes well beyond the English league:

NicknameClubOrigin
The VillansAston VillaFrom the club's name, itself from Villa Cross
The GunnersArsenalFrom the Royal Arsenal armament factory, the club's birthplace
The PiesChorleyFrom the town's famous pie-making tradition
The BladesSheffield UnitedSheffield's cutlery industry
The IronScunthorpe UnitedSteel and ironworks of the town
The SilkmenMacclesfieldMacclesfield's silk industry
The GloversYeovil TownGlove-making industry of Somerset
La Dea (The Goddess)AtalantaFrom Atalanta, the goddess of Greek mythology
The HorsemenQarabagFrom the Karabakh horses of the region
The pattern: Most strange nicknames come from three places — a local industry (the Iron, the Silkmen), a local food (the Pies, the Tangerines) or an accident of history (the Addicks, the Owls). A nickname only feels strange until you know the town.

Club identity runs deep, and nicknames are a big part of it. For more on football identity, see why some clubs play in unusual colours.
